t: #3895 Good Subsequence Queries — GCD Structure with Segment Tree
o: After each point update, decide whether some proper (length < n) subsequence has GCD exactly p. Any valid subsequence uses only elements divisible by p; dividing those by p, we need a subsequence of the transformed array with GCD 1, of size < n. Let c = count of p-divisible elements and g = GCD of their divided values. If g > 1, impossible. If g == 1 and c < n, take all of them — yes. If c == n, we need to drop one element while keeping GCD 1; crucially, whenever a set has GCD 1, some subset of size <= log2(max value) ≈ 17 already has GCD 1 (each added element at least halves the GCD), so for n >= 17 the answer is automatically yes, and only tiny arrays need an explicit drop-one check. A segment tree over the transformed array supports point updates and GCD queries.
k: Transform b[i] = nums[i]/p if p divides nums[i], else 0 (identity for GCD); the question becomes: exists subset of size < n with GCD 1.
If GCD of all nonzero b is 1 and fewer than n of them are nonzero, the answer is immediately yes.
GCD-1 certificates are tiny: some <= 17 elements always suffice, so for n >= 17 the c == n case is always yes; only n <= 17 needs an O(n) drop-one scan.
A segment tree gives O(log n) point update and range GCD.

a.n: Approach 1: Rebuild prefix/suffix GCDs per query
a.i: After each update, recompute the transformed array, its total GCD and nonzero count, and — when needed — prefix/suffix GCD arrays to test dropping each single element. O(n) per query; simple and a good baseline.
s: Build b[i] = nums[i]/p if divisible else 0; compute g = GCD of all b and c = count of nonzero.
If g != 1, no good subsequence exists.
If c < n, yes. Otherwise check whether dropping some index leaves GCD 1 via prefix/suffix GCD arrays.
a.t: O(n * q) — full recomputation per query; 2.5e9 worst case, so it may TLE at maximal constraints.

a.n: Approach 2: Segment tree GCD + small-n certificate bound
a.i: Maintain the transformed array in a GCD segment tree. Per query: O(log n) update, O(log n) total-GCD query, and the drop-one check only runs when c == n and n <= 17 (otherwise the <=17-element certificate bound makes the answer trivially yes). This gives near-linear total time.
s: Build a segment tree where leaf i holds nums[i]/p (or 0 if not divisible); internal nodes hold GCD, with 0 as identity.
On update, fix the leaf and propagate GCDs upward; maintain the count of divisible elements.
Per query: if total GCD != 1, answer no. Else if c < n or n >= 17, answer yes.
Otherwise (tiny n) test each drop position with two range-GCD queries.
a.t: O((n + q) log n) for tree operations, plus O(n log n) drop-one checks only when n <= 17.

w: The two non-obvious facts carry this problem: (1) a GCD-1 set always contains a GCD-1 subset of size <= log2(max value), and (2) elements not divisible by p can never join a GCD-p subsequence. Pitfalls: forgetting the size < n restriction when c == n, and mishandling 0 as the GCD identity. Follow-up: report the actual subsequence, or handle range updates.
